title: Do You Watch Too Many Revenge Films
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership warns that repeated exposure to revenge narratives can subtly reshape a leader's internal script for power and justice. Leaders who consume a steady diet of revenge films and books become more likely to normalize grievance, see conflicts through an us-versus-them lens, and become subtly more aggressive and punitive over time. The crucial distinction is between accountability (corrective, forward-looking, about standards) and revenge (punitive, past-focused, about settling a score). The article argues that when a leader is seen exacting retribution, team members perceive them as less trustworthy and more unfair, whereas leaders who favor reconciliation and fairness over retaliation foster higher trust and transparency.
points: Repeated exposure to revenge narratives trains a leader's internal script for how power and justice are handled; fiction shapes behavior over time.
Accountability is corrective and forward-looking (elevates performance); revenge is punitive and past-focused (settles a score).
When teams witness a leader retaliate, they view that leader as less trustworthy and more unfair, regardless of how justified the action seems in the moment.
Leaders who favor reconciliation and fairness over retaliation promote higher trust, openness, and transparency from their team.
Good leaders never cross the line between holding people accountable and exacting revenge; competence and credibility create any symbolic payoff they need.
quotes: Thoughts of revenge can channel complex emotions—anger, grief, humiliation, and power—into a controlled narrative with closure.
Reclaiming power through decisive action is invigorating to watch and think about for many people. No wonder revenge movies are one of the more popular film genres.

Unlike real life, the conflict is resolved permanently, and the sense of order that the real world often denies is reaffirmed. Unfortunately, repeated exposure to revenge narratives has been shown to heighten moral polarization and desensitize empathy.

Leaders who expose themselves to a steady diet of revenge movies and books are more likely to normalize grievance, see conflicts through an 'us versus them' lens, and become subtly more aggressive and punitive in their behavior over time.
The risk is not that fictional stories reinforce bad instincts, but that repeated exposure trains a leader's internal script for how power, justice, and respect are to be handled.
Good leaders don't seek revenge. They recognize that retaliatory behavior is a personal, emotional, and backward-looking reaction.

Accountability is corrective and forward-looking, while revenge is punitive and past-focused. Accountability is about establishing standards and elevating long-term performance, while revenge is about settling a score and inflicting pain.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
